archetype.name: Rebuilding (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team in its third straight bottom-tier season whose defense and line keep it in games while an offense near the bottom of the league decides most of them the wrong way.

report.headline: A competitive defense keeps games close; an offense ranked near the bottom can't finish them.
report.take:
Tennessee is 1-5, but this is not the same team that went 3-14 the last two years. The 2025 group gave up 28.1 points a game and ranked 31st in net EPA. This one allows 21.5, 13th in the league, and most of its losses have come down to the final possession: Philadelphia by four, the Giants by five, Baltimore by six. The point differential implies about 1.9 wins, so the record undersells the team a little. Not by much, though. A -0.155 net EPA (29th) is still a bad team, just a more respectable one.

The passing offense is what sinks it. Tennessee ranks 30th in pass EPA, 31st in total offensive EPA and 31st in scoring at 14 points a game. The staff has responded by hiding the pass. Their pass rate over expected of -8.5 is 30th, and Tony Pollard's 87 carries far outnumber anyone else's. The line has done its part on the ground, with the league's lowest stuff rate and an 85.7% conversion rate in short yardage, but the run game is only average per play (3.68 yards a carry, 18th in run EPA). That leaves Cam Ward throwing into obvious passing downs. Some weeks the result is survivable, as at Baltimore. Other weeks it collapses: -16.9 pass EPA in the 3-26 loss to Houston. Tennessee is also last in time of possession, so even a run-first plan isn't keeping the defense off the field.

The defense itself is split. Against the run it is sound: 13th in rush EPA allowed, with the league's second-lowest missed-tackle rate. Offenses respond by running at it anyway. Its pass-rate-over-norm of -7 makes it the league's strongest run funnel, and that has kept the back end from being tested as often as it deserves. When teams do throw, the coverage leaks badly, ranking 26th in pass EPA allowed and 26th on deep balls. The sack total (16, 9th) flatters a pass rush that ranks 30th in pressure rate. Six of those sacks came in last week's win at Indianapolis, a game that also brought three takeaways after five games with only two.

The direction is toward a tougher, more competitive loser rather than a team about to turn the corner. Every one of Ward's dropbacks still carries real risk. The secondary is about to lose Kevin Winston Jr., an every-snap safety. The Indianapolis formula of a pass rush and turnovers carrying a 102-yard passing day is not one a team can count on repeating.

strengths.title: Disciplined, sure-tackling run defense
strengths.body: Tennessee tackles well and fits the run soundly, ranking second in missed-tackle rate and 13th in rush EPA allowed. That is a big reason points allowed fell from 28.1 a game last year to 21.5. It rests on technique and structure rather than turnovers, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Line wins at the point of attack
strengths.body: Tennessee's runners are rarely hit in the backfield (stuff rate 1st), the team converts short yardage (4th), and Ward is rarely hit (QB hit rate allowed 2nd). Saleh leans on this with fourth-down aggression. It is a real foundation for a run-first, ball-control plan, even though it hasn't produced explosive gains.

strengths.title: Low penalties, close games
strengths.body: At 6.3 penalties a game, fifth-fewest in the league, Tennessee rarely beats itself with flags. Combined with the run defense, that keeps most games within one score. The flip side is a 0.25 one-score win rate, which has more room to rise than fall.

concerns.title: The passing game is near the bottom
concerns.body: Tennessee ranks 30th in pass EPA, and its run-heavy pass rate over expected is a way of protecting Ward, not an identity built on strength. The offense ranks 32nd in time of possession, so the run-first plan isn't sustaining drives either. Until the dropbacks become neutral rather than damaging, 14 points a game is about the ceiling.

concerns.title: Leaky coverage, now short a safety
concerns.body: The pass defense ranks 26th in EPA allowed and 26th against deep throws, and it has been protected by opponents choosing to run. Losing Winston, an every-snap safety, with Tony Adams also questionable, puts more strain on the weakest unit of the defense.

concerns.title: Sacks outrunning the pressure
concerns.body: Tennessee's pressure rate ranks 30th, yet its sack rate ranks 7th. That gap usually narrows, especially when six of the 16 sacks came in a single game. Takeaways are also scarce (27th), so the defense doesn't create short fields to help the offense.

trend.note: The profile has barely moved week to week: low scoring, a competitive defense and mostly one-score losses, with the Houston blowout as the outlier. The win at Indianapolis came from six sacks and three takeaways rather than any change in the offense, which threw for 102 yards.

nextGame.headline: Two weak offenses, and a Browns line Tennessee's rush can hit.
nextGame.body:
The Book has Cleveland as a 1.5-point road favorite with a 38.5 total, essentially a coin flip. That is fair: the Browns' 4-2 record rests on a 0.8 one-score win rate and the league's third-highest wins over expected, while their point differential ranks 23rd. Cleveland's offense is nearly as broken as Tennessee's. It ranks 31st in run EPA and allows the league's highest sack rate, so it leans on Deshaun Watson's arm (sixth in pass rate over expected). That pass-first approach aims straight at Tennessee's weakest unit. Cleveland's defense is the better group, ranking 10th in EPA, fourth in sack rate and fifth in red-zone TD rate allowed. Its weakness is the run, where it gives up explosive runs at the league's highest rate and misses too many tackles.

Availability favors Tennessee up front and hurts it at the back. Cleveland is without three defensive tackles (Mason Graham and Mike Hall Jr. out, Kalia Davis on IR). It is also missing Quinshon Judkins, Dylan Sampson and guard Teven Jenkins, and safety Grant Delpit is questionable with a concussion. That combination thins the interior run defense and makes the Browns' already weak run game weaker. Tennessee loses safety Kevin Winston Jr. and DT Jordan Elliott, with Tony Adams questionable, which matters most against a Browns offense that wants to throw.

waysToWin.title: Pin its ears back against Cleveland's line
waysToWin.body: Cleveland allows a sack on 10.8% of dropbacks, the worst rate in the league, and Tennessee's rush is coming off a six-sack game. Cleveland can't run the ball, so Watson will be throwing in obvious passing situations. That is where even a low-pressure front can turn sacks into short drives and punts.

waysToWin.title: Pound the ball at a depleted interior
waysToWin.body: Three Cleveland defensive tackles are out, and the Browns allow explosive runs more often than any defense in the league. Tennessee's line, with the league's lowest stuff rate, can lean on Pollard and keep Ward out of long passing downs. One caution: Cleveland has held lead backs well below their usual output, so Tennessee has to win up front rather than assume the yards will come.

waysToWin.title: Out-discipline a flag-prone opponent
waysToWin.body: Cleveland commits 9.2 penalties a game, 30th in the league, against Tennessee's fifth-cleanest 6.3. In a game with a 38.5 total, a few free first downs could decide it, and Saleh's willingness to go for it on fourth down can turn those extended drives into points.

waysToLose.title: Watson finds the thinned secondary
waysToLose.body: Cleveland passes more than expected, and Tennessee ranks 26th in pass EPA allowed and 26th on deep throws. The Titans will be missing Winston and possibly Adams. A couple of completions over the top in a low-scoring game would be hard for Tennessee's offense to answer.

waysToLose.title: Cleveland's rush wrecks Ward's dropbacks
waysToLose.body: The Browns rank fourth in sack rate and fifth in QB hit rate. Tennessee's line allows pressure at the 25th-ranked rate even though it limits hits. If the Titans fall behind the sticks, the Houston script (-16.9 pass EPA, four sacks) is the risk.

waysToLose.title: Settling for field goals
waysToLose.body: Cleveland allows touchdowns on just 43.8% of red-zone trips, fifth-best in the league. Tennessee's special teams have been costing it 2.26 points of EPA a game. Kicking field goals while giving away hidden yardage is how a field-position game slips away.

nextGame.watch: Tennessee's sack-and-takeaway rate on Watson's dropbacks: against the league's leakiest pass protection, it is the Titans' clearest path to a short field and a second straight win.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense's improvement looks real. It is built on run fits and tackling rather than turnovers, and it should keep Tennessee in more games than the last two 3-14 teams. The one-score win rate of 0.25 also has room to tick up. What won't hold is the sack production relative to a 30th-ranked pressure rate, and the secondary gets weaker with Winston out. The schedule brings several top-ten offenses (Jacksonville twice, Detroit, Dallas, Cincinnati), which will test that coverage more than the run-funnel opponents have.

The offense is the ceiling. A few defenses ahead rank near the bottom of the league (Detroit 32nd, Dallas 31st, Washington 26th), which gives Ward chances for better passing days. Still, nothing in six games suggests the passing game will reach league average. Expect a team that loses close more often than it wins close, steals a few games against weak defenses and division rivals, and finishes in the bottom handful of the league again, though with a clearly better point differential than 2025.
swingFactors: Whether Ward's dropbacks improve from damaging to neutral
How long the secondary plays without Winston

confidence.note: Six games, but a consistent profile with no QB change.
